title: Canada Joins UK-Led GCAP Fighter Jet Programme as Western Allies Pivot From US Defence
excerpt: Ottawa becomes the first observer nation in the sixth-generation stealth fighter project developed by Britain, Italy, and Japan, as the Farnborough Airshow showcases a defence sector shaped by conflict and shifting alliances.
body:
• Canada joined the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) as its first observer nation, gaining access to the UK-Italy-Japan stealth fighter project without any financial commitment.
  • New UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's cabinet appointments — John Healey as finance minister and Wes Streeting as defence secretary — boosted British defence and aerospace stocks.
  • The move is part of Canada's broader push to diversify defence spending away from the United States, after slashing its F-35 order from 88 jets to 16.
  • Defence companies made up half of a record 1,600 exhibitors at the Farnborough Airshow, reflecting how wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are reshaping global military spending.

Canada has joined the Global Combat Air Programme as its first observer nation, marking the programme's first expansion beyond its three founding members and handing Britain's new government an early diplomatic win at the Farnborough Airshow.

The announcement came on Tuesday as newly appointed UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting hosted his Japanese, Italian, and Canadian counterparts on his first full day in the role. Canada will gain direct insight into GCAP's capability development, industrial collaboration, and long-term delivery plans, though the observer status carries no financial commitment, according to Reuters.

"GCAP continues to strengthen our security, drive technological innovation and create highly skilled jobs across the UK. We are proud to welcome Canada to this new phase of engagement."

— Wes Streeting, UK Defence Secretary

A New Government's Defence Gambit

The GCAP expansion coincides with Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first days in office. Burnham named John Healey, who had spent months lobbying the previous government to commit 3% of GDP to defence by 2030, as finance minister, while handing Streeting — previously the health minister — the defence portfolio.

Markets responded positively. British defence and aerospace stocks rose on Tuesday as investors bet on the new government's willingness to increase military spending, according to Reuters. BAE Systems CEO Charles Woodburn praised Healey's track record, saying he had "championed British business, recognising the contribution that the defence sector makes to growth and national security."

Rolls-Royce CEO Tufan Erginbilgic struck a similar note at the airshow, telling reporters: "He understands Rolls-Royce and our agenda and how much we contribute to the country."

The government also faces a £4.7 billion defence funding gap inherited from the Starmer administration, which had committed an additional £15 billion to defence but identified sources for only two-thirds of that sum.

Canada's Strategic Pivot Away From Washington

For Ottawa, joining GCAP represents another step in a deliberate diversification of defence partnerships away from the United States. Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Canada has slashed its order of American-made F-35 jets from 88 to just 16 and is evaluating Swedish-made Gripen E fighters as an alternative, according to The Sun.

Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty described GCAP as a "promising initiative" and said the partnership proved that allies are "stronger together." He told Reuters last month that he had discussed the programme with Japan's defence minister in Tokyo, laying the groundwork for Tuesday's announcement.

"This isn't about leverage. The message is, we are stronger together."

— David McGuinty, Canadian Defence Minister

The shift follows months of trade tensions between Ottawa and Washington, including tariff threats from President Trump. Carney has pledged to reduce Canada's defence purchases from the US, where roughly 70% of its military budget was previously spent.

The Broader Defence Landscape

GCAP, launched in 2022 by Britain, Italy, and Japan, aims to produce a sixth-generation stealth fighter by 2035. It is one of two major Western next-generation fighter programmes alongside the US Air Force's Next Generation Air Dominance project. The programme is led by BAE Systems, Japan's Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and Italy's Leonardo.

At Farnborough, defence companies accounted for half of a record 1,600 exhibitors, underscoring how the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have reshaped spending priorities. BAE Systems, Boeing, and Saab also signed a deal at the show to develop a fast-jet pilot training aircraft based on Boeing's T-7 system, as the UK seeks a replacement for its ageing Hawk fleet.

For Indian defence watchers, the realignment carries implications. As Canada and European nations move to reduce dependence on US military hardware, the shift could open new avenues for defence cooperation between India and its traditional partners in Europe and Japan, while reshaping the competitive landscape for India's own growing defence exports.

What Comes Next

While Canada's observer status involves no financial commitment, it paves the way for a more formal role in the future — potentially sharing the programme's billion-dollar development costs and ordering the jets. The UK government must also resolve its inherited defence funding shortfall, with the remaining £4.7 billion expected to be addressed in an upcoming budget. The Farnborough Airshow continues through July 24, with further defence and commercial aviation announcements expected.
